title: Logical Entangling with Phantom Codes in Hypergraph Products
authors: Keming He, Ziao Tang, Zetong Li, Ge Bai, Xin Wang
abstract: Logical entangling gates are a major source of physical spacetime overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computation. Phantom codes reduce this cost by implementing every ordered in-block logical CNOT through physical qubit permutations and Pauli-frame updates. Whether this mechanism can coexist with the low-weight stabilizer structure of qLDPC codes is a central question for low-overhead fault-tolerant architectures. We give a deterministic answer within binary CSS hypergraph product (HGP) codes. Up to natural equivalences, the simplex-repetition family is the unique HGP family satisfying the phantom condition. We then evaluate this family under circuit-level noise in logical GHZ-state preparation and Trotterized many-body quantum simulation. The codes retain low-weight stabilizer checks and yield concrete advantages over rotated surface-code baselines in both benchmarks. Reconfigurable neutral-atom arrays offer a natural setting for this approach, supporting nonlocal qLDPC operations while enabling in-block logical CNOTs without additional physical operations. Together, these results make precise how permutation-based logical entangling constrains code design within the HGP framework, demonstrate the circuit-level benefits of the unique family, and guide the search for phantom qLDPC families with better asymptotic parameters for low-overhead fault tolerance on neutral-atom hardware.
summary: This paper theoretically classifies Hypergraph Product (HGP) codes that minimize overhead during logical entanglement gate implementation by requiring the use of physical qubit permutations. The unique resulting family is then rigorously benchmarked against surface codes in simulating complex quantum circuits, demonstrating concrete performance advantages for low-overhead fault tolerance on hardware like neutral-atom arrays.
main_problem: The primary goal is reducing physical spacetime overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computation by finding efficient ways to implement logical entangling gates.
main_result: The authors prove that the only Hypergraph Product (HGP) codes satisfying the 'phantom' condition are derived from a simplex code and a repetition code, which outperform surface codes in benchmark simulations.
method: The work combines theoretical classification of CSS HGP codes based on permutation automorphisms with extensive circuit-level benchmarking using Monte Carlo simulations for GHZ state preparation and many-body simulation.
model_or_system: The study focuses on Quantum Error Correction (QEC) using binary CSS Hypergraph Product (HGP) codes, specifically the simplex–repetition family. These codes are evaluated in the context of implementing logical CNOT gates via physical qubit permutations.
key_observables: Logical infidelity ($1 - F$), which measures the average mismatch probability per target logical observable; code parameters like distance ($d$) and number of qubits ($n$).
important_parameters: Physical error rates ($p = 10^{-3}, 5 	imes 10^{-4}$); system sizes (up to $K=64$ logical qubits).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the physical realization of the HGP structure and uses a specific noise model for circuit simulations; it also notes that the results are up to natural equivalences.
figures_summary: Figures compare logical GHZ-state preparation fidelity and Trotterized many-body simulation fidelity between the proposed HGP code and rotated surface codes, showing consistent outperformance of the HGP code.
paper_structure: The paper first theoretically classifies the unique structure of phantom CSS HGP codes (Theorem 2), then derives the specific simplex–repetition family using weight analysis (Theorem 3), and finally validates this family by benchmarking its performance against surface codes in two distinct quantum simulation tasks.
why_interesting: The direct comparison with neutral-atom arrays as a natural hardware setting, which supports nonlocal qLDPC operations while enabling the required local CNOTs via permutations, makes this highly relevant for experimental AMO physicists working on scalable quantum computation.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic illustration of the simplex–repetition HGP phan- tom code. The gray funnel represents the classification result. Up to natural equivalences, the phantom condition selects the simplex– repetition family among binary CSS HGP constructions. The two classical seed codes H1, H2 are the simplex code and the repetition code. Their hypergraph product gives the corresponding HGP phan- tom code. Black dots denote physical qubits, while orange and blue squares denote X- and Z-checks, respectively. Orange arrows depict a physical qubit permutation π. For each ordered in-block logical CNOT, an appropriate permutation π and a Pauli-frame update real- ize the logical operation.

FIG. 2. Logical GHZ-state preparation with the simplex–repetition HGP phantom family. Left: p = 5 × 10−4. Right: p = 10−3. For each K-qubit GHZ target, HGP data use K/4 four-logical-qubit phantom blocks, whereas the surface-code baseline uses K rotated surface-code blocks. HGP distances are d = 5, 6, 7, 8, and surface- code baselines use d = 6, 8. The HGP implementation absorbs in-block CNOTs into phantom relabellings, leaving only transver- sal inter-block CNOT layers followed by QEC cycles.

FIG. 3. Trotterized many-body benchmark. Left: p = 5 × 10−4. Right: p = 10−3. The HGP and surface-code configurations match those of the GHZ benchmark: K/4 four-logical-qubit HGP phantom blocks are compared with K rotated surface-code blocks, using HGP distances d = 5, 6, 7, 8 and surface-code distances d = 6, 8.
